We used iterated decomposition and ICE to improve performance over simple baselines on three real-world case studies
we encountered in our work on Elicit (Figure 4).

These applications serve as case studies for a workflow that, if automated, could keep ML systems
interpretable and safe even as they scale to increasingly complex tasks.

method.description: A developer-designed decomposition (classify from the trial arms with rank-and-answer steps, classify from each paragraph and aggregate, then ensemble the two) was compared with the Elicit select-then-generate baseline on a held-out test set (Table 2, classification n=48), and execution traces were then reviewed in ICE.

passages.text:
In outline, the decomposition looks like this:
1. Classify based on trial arms
(a) What were the trial arms?
i. Rank paragraphs by relevance to this question through pairwise comparisons
ii. Answer based on the most relevant paragraphs
(b) Describe each trial arm: Rank and Answer
(c) Do any of the arms look like placebos?
(d) If so, could participants tell which arm they were in? (If so, there’s not really a placebo.)
2. Classify based on each paragraph
(a) Was there a placebo, according to each paragraph?
(b) Aggregate answers from paragraphs
3. Ensemble the classification based on trial arms and paragraphs

passages.text:
Case Study: Placebo Classification & Description

In this case study, we focus on domain-specific decompositions. Through iteration on the classification and description
steps, accuracy of the generated placebo description improved from 25% to 65% on a held-out test set.
4.1

Setup

Given the full text of an RCT, the task is to answer “Did this RCT use a placebo?” (classification) and “If so, what was
it?” (description). For both classification and description we find strong agreement among human raters.
On a held-out test set, this approach has 71% accuracy for classification, 25% for description (Table 2).

Besides helping researchers evaluate risk of bias, another reason to pick this task was that it is a fairly easy task. We
wanted to try decomposition in a setting where success was likely, and identify any unexpected failure modes.

setting.systems: A compositional LM program; the baseline ranks paragraphs with monoT5 and answers with text-davinci-002
setting.task_data: Placebo classification ('Did this RCT use a placebo?') from full texts of randomized controlled trials

quantitative.uncertainty: p = 0.0004 for 71% → 98%; the test used is not named in these passages

limits.notes: The authors chose the task as fairly easy; the gain is attributed almost entirely to the paragraph-wise classification rather than the trial-arms branch.

strength.reason: A single case study on one held-out test set (n=48); a p-value is reported, but the rubric grades a result resting on a case study as preliminary, and the authors chose the task as fairly easy.

method.description: The placebo description was generated by ranking paragraphs by relevance through pairwise comparisons and answering from the most relevant ones (the same Rank and Answer step used for classification), and compared with the Elicit baseline on trials that used a placebo, each description checked against the gold standard (Table 2, n=20).

1. Classify based on trial arms
(a) What were the trial arms?
i. Rank paragraphs by relevance to this question through pairwise comparisons
ii. Answer based on the most relevant paragraphs
(b) Describe each trial arm: Rank and Answer

We evaluate each trial, rather than the paper. A trial is when participants are randomized into arms that will be tested
against each other. Some papers discuss multiple trials, and sometimes some trials are blinded while others are not.
There are 61 experiments in our test set across 47 papers.
To evaluate placebo descriptions, we only look at experiments where there is in fact a placebo. If the decompositino
said that there is no placebo, we immediately count that description as wrong. Otherwise, we check whether the
decomposition’s description is reasonably accurate and complete compared to the gold standard.

method.description: Starting from the Elicit select-then-generate baseline, the authors iterated on the selection step (a zero-shot perplexity classifier) and the generation step (few-shot answering from expert demonstrations) and measured accuracy against gold standards on held-out test sets for experiments, arms and adherence (Table 3).

passages.text:
The zero-shot perplexity classifier and few-shot answering via “demonstrations” add up to substantial improvements
over the Elicit baseline (e.g. 53% correct → 70% for adherence, p=0.0065 ; see Table 3). These techniques vastly reduce
the number of false negatives for the adherence task (error analysis in Appendix 9.6.3).

Experiments and arms are relatively easy to evaluate—we can check whether each experiment/arm from the gold
standard is represented and whether there are any additional ones that should not be there.
Adherence tends to require a narrative answer, and to be more subjective. This means that it may benefit more from a
nuanced decomposition, and approaches that work well for adherence may generalize better to other fuzzy tasks.
Each arm has an adherence answer, so there are a total of 135 adherence answers in our test set. Often, no information
about adherence is available in the text of the paper—information about adherence is only available for 56/135 arms
(41%) in our test set. So the adherence task is substantially a classification task (adherence mentioned vs. not mentioned).

passages.text:
We generated few-shot prompts from expert demonstrations (gold standards) by prepending the existing perplexity
selection prompt with multiple filled examples. We either used only positive demonstrations, which included a
supporting paragraph and an expert’s handwritten answer based on that paragraph, or mixed positive and negative
demonstrations, which assumed that unmarked paragraphs did not answer the question. This assumption was often
false, so we found it better to use only positive examples in the few-shot demonstration prompts.
Across all tasks, the few-shot prompts derived from demonstrations improved the accuracy of generation over the
zero-shot approach, even with randomly sampled examples from the development set. The improvement was larger

method.description: The select-then-generate baselines and the best participant-flow decompositions (perplexity selection with and without few-shot demonstrations) were run on 100 sampled Qasper questions, and each answer was rated as semantically equivalent to the expert answers or not, with F1 also reported (Table 4).

passages.text:
We tested both our select-then-generate baselines and our best-performing decompositions (perplexity selection, with
and without few-shot examples from demonstrations) on a sample of Q ASPER questions. Table 4 shows the results.

Because we care about correctness of answers, not whether they literally match expert wording, we focused instead on
a binary assessment of whether the generated answer was semantically equivalent to the expert answers. For example, a
yes-no answer of “yes” versus a generated answer of “true” would have F1 = 0, but we would rate it as correct. For
completeness, we also measure and report F1 scores, but we did not adapt decompositions to maximize F1 .
To keep the task and assessments manageable but meaningful, we sampled 100 questions from Q ASPER to test both
baselines and decompositions that performed substantially better than baselines on the participant flow tasks. We
performed light data cleaning before testing, removing special tokens indicating cross-references with natural language
equivalents (e.g., converting ‘BIBREF0’ to ‘[1]’) and, as in the original Q ASPER paper, omitting questions that required
tables or figures to answer.

Table 4: Results for the Q ASPER NLP question-answering task (n=100). The ordering of methods by performance is
the same as for the participant flow case study, providing some evidence of generality for decompositions.

stated_hypotheses: The decompositions were iterated on primarily using the earlier case-study tasks and then tested on Qasper to see how well they generalise.
Accuracy is a binary rating of semantic equivalence to the expert answers, not F1; decompositions were not adapted to maximise F1.
100 questions are sampled; questions that need tables or figures are omitted.
Few-shot demonstrations are other, randomly selected Qasper question-paragraph-answer tuples.

passages.text:
Case Study: Q ASPER NLP question answering

We primarily iterated on decompositions using the tasks above. However, we also wanted to explore how well these
task decompositions generalized to other domains and questions, so we tested them on a subset of the Q ASPER dataset,
a question-answering dataset of 5,049 questions and answers written by NLP practitioners, covering 1,585 NLP papers
(Dasigi et al., 2021). By using the final decomposition for participant flow, accuracy at answering NLP questions on the
Q ASPER dataset improved from 38% to 69%.

setting.systems: LM select-then-generate programs (perplexity classifier, optional few-shot demonstrations)
setting.task_data: A sample of 100 questions from Qasper, a dataset of questions about NLP papers answered by NLP practitioners
setting.judge: The authors rate whether each answer is semantically equivalent to the expert answers

quantitative.uncertainty: 'Significantly outperformed' is stated without a named test, p-value or interval

limits.notes: One sample of 100 questions; the authors hedge that the decomposition is 'somewhat robust' to domain transfer, giving 'some evidence of generality'.

strength.reason: The authors present this as a case study ('Case Study: QASPER NLP question answering') on one sample of 100 questions; 'significantly' is backed by no stated test, p-value or interval, and the authors hedge the result as 'some evidence of generality'. The rubric grades a result resting on a case study as preliminary.
